claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials are governed by a load-induced thermo-plastic instability that triggers a clustering-to-ordering transition.
High-strain compression of Al0.1CrCoFeNi at elevated temperature induces a clustering-to-ordering transition.
The compression-induced ordering is evidenced by increased unlike-pair correlations, including Al-Co and Al-Cr, and reduced like-pair correlations.
Tensile loading does not induce the clustering-to-ordering transition.
Local thermo-plastic instabilities under compression promote the transition from a clustered disordered state to an ordered atomic configuration.
The ordered atomic configuration enhances dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning increases strain hardening.
The increased strain hardening delays failure and increases toughness.
Tensile loading produces lower flow stress, lower strain hardening, and reduced ductility relative to compressive loading at the same temperature.
A rapidly quenched Al0.1CrCoFeNi-like high-entropy alloy can begin in an FCC, disordered solid-solution state exhibiting atomistic clustering.
Compression between 700 K and 1000 K will produce higher post-yield flow stress than tension or low-deformation baselines.
Compression between 700 K and 1000 K will produce greater strain hardening and toughness than tension or low-deformation baselines.
The cited compression behavior occurs over temperatures of 700 K to 1000 K.
Temperatures of 700 K to 1000 K are representative of fusion plasma-facing environments.
The hypothesized mechanism applies generally to complex concentrated alloys that have metastable clustering in their as-processed state.
The mechanism may not apply to simpler alloys or compounds lacking clustering behavior.
Differences between computational and experimental loading rates may change the magnitude of the ordering effect.
